title: Automation: macros, Office Scripts and Python

lessons.title: Record and run a macro on Mac
learn: Save as .xlsm, assign to a button
lessons.mac:
• Developer tab: Excel > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar
• Tools > Macro > Record New Macro / Macros…
• Shortcut keys: ⌥ + ⌘ + a letter
• Excel > Preferences > Security: allow macros with a warning
• Excel for the web and iPad cannot run VBA macros

steps.say: Every morning the system gives you a plain sales export. This is the same report after one click on a macro: a coloured header, rupee formatting, neat columns and a frozen top row. You record the steps once, and Excel repeats them every day.

You will learn to show the Developer tab, record a macro, run it on a new day's data, and save the file so the macro isn't lost. Practice sheets S16-01 and S16-01 Day2. This is recorded in Excel desktop, and I'll give the Mac menus as we go.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Show the Developer tab
2. Record a macro (absolute vs relative references)
3. Run it on new data
4. Save as .xlsm and add a button

Practice: sheets S16-01 and S16-01 Day2

steps.say: A macro is a recording of your clicks and keystrokes, saved as VBA code. By default it remembers exact cells. With Use Relative References switched on, it remembers moves relative to where you started instead.

acts.t:
Macro basics

Record Macro → do the steps → Stop Recording
Absolute (default): 'select A1:F1' every time
Relative: 'move 1 cell right' from wherever you start
Macros live in the workbook: save as .xlsm (Macro-Enabled)

steps.say: First, show the Developer tab. On a Mac, open the Excel menu, choose Preferences, then Ribbon and Toolbar, tick Developer and click Save. On Windows it is File, Options, Customize Ribbon.

acts.t:
Show the Developer tab (once)

Mac: Excel > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar > tick Developer > Save
Windows: File > Options > Customize Ribbon > tick Developer

Mac menu bar alternative: Tools > Macro > Record New Macro

steps.say: Go to sheet S16-01 and click A1. On the Developer tab you'll see Use Relative References. Our report always starts at A1, so we leave it off and record exact cells.
Click Record Macro. Name it FormatDailyReport, with no spaces. Store it in This Workbook, and click OK. From now on, every click is recorded, so work calmly.

acts.h: Set Store macro in to This Workbook

steps.say: Select A1 to F1 and press Command B for bold. Set the fill colour to dark blue and the font colour to white.
Select the whole of column F, press Command 1, choose Custom, and type the rupee lakh format. Click OK.
Select columns A to F, and on the Home tab choose Format, AutoFit Column Width. Then on the View tab choose Freeze Panes, Freeze Top Row. Click A1 to finish neatly.
On the Developer tab, click Stop Recording. The macro is saved inside this workbook.
Now the payoff. Go to sheet S16-01 Day2, tomorrow's raw export. On the Developer tab, click Macros, choose FormatDailyReport and click Run. The whole report is formatted in a second.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S16-01 Day2

steps.say: Here's the mistake that loses people their work. Press Command S. Excel warns that macros can't be saved in a macro-free workbook. If you click Yes, the file saves as xlsx and the macro is gone. Click No instead.
In the Save As box, set the file type to Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook, which ends in xlsm, and click Save. The macro is now kept with the file.

acts.h: Set Save as type to Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook (*.xlsm)

steps.say: To give colleagues a one-click button, choose Developer, Button, draw it on the sheet, and pick FormatDailyReport in the Assign Macro box. Right-click the button to rename it Format report.

acts.t:
Add a button

1. Developer > Button (Form Control)
2. Drag to draw it on the sheet
3. Assign Macro: FormatDailyReport > OK
4. Control-click the button > Edit Text: 'Format report'

Mac: Developer > Button works the same way

steps.say: On a Mac, you can also record from the menu bar with Tools, Macro, Record New Macro. Macro shortcut keys use Option and Command. Check Excel, Preferences, Security, so macros are allowed to run with a warning. Excel for the web can't run VBA at all.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Developer tab: Excel > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar
• Tools > Macro > Record New Macro / Macros…
• Shortcut keys: ⌥ + ⌘ + a letter
• Excel > Preferences > Security: allow macros with a warning
• Excel for the web and iPad cannot run VBA macros

steps.say: To recap: show the Developer tab, record carefully, stop recording. Run the macro on new data from the Macros box or a button. Always save as xlsm.

acts.t:
Recap

• Developer > Record Macro → steps → Stop Recording
• Run: Developer > Macros, or a button
• Save as .xlsm, or the macro is lost

steps.say: Your challenge: record a second macro with Use Relative References switched on, that bolds the cell you're in and the two cells to its right. Run it from different starting cells. The explanation is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Turn on Use Relative References, record 'BoldThree': bold the active cell and the next two to the right.
Run it from C5, then from A10. What happens?

Answer: sheet S16-01 Done, cell H5

lessons.title: Reading and editing VBA
lessons.mac:
• VBE: ⌥ + F11 or Tools > Macro > Visual Basic Editor
• Insert > Module · Run: F5 (fn + F5) · Edit > Replace (⌃ + H)
• Back to Excel: ⌥ + F11 or click the Excel window
• Some Windows-only objects fail on Mac (lesson S16-04)

steps.say: This payroll report was formatted by a macro we opened, read and improved by hand. The header colour was changed in the code, and the cleaner version works on a report of any size. You don't need to be a programmer to do this.

You will learn to open the Visual Basic Editor, read what a recorded macro does line by line, fix an error, and change it safely with Find and Replace. Practice sheet S16-02, recorded in Excel desktop.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. The Visual Basic Editor (VBE)
2. Read a recorded macro line by line
3. A cleaner version, a run-time error and its fix
4. Edit safely with Replace

Practice: sheet S16-02

steps.say: Every macro sits between Sub and End Sub. Most lines follow one pattern: an object, a dot, a property, equals, a value. Lines starting with an apostrophe are comments, shown in green, and Excel ignores them.

acts.t:
Reading VBA

Sub FormatReport() … End Sub   ← one macro
Range("A1:F1").Font.Bold = True
  object  .  property  =  value
' comment (green, ignored)
With … End With   ← several properties of one object

Mac: Tools > Macro > Visual Basic Editor (⌥ + F11)

steps.say: Go to sheet S16-02 and press Option F11 on a Mac, or Alt F11 on Windows, to open the Visual Basic Editor. On the Insert menu, choose Module. A blank code window opens.
Here is the macro the recorder wrote for this report. I'll type it in. Notice that End Sub appears by itself as soon as you finish the first line.

acts.h: Type Sub FormatReport() ' Recorded macro: formats the payroll report Range("A1:F1").Select Selection.Font.Bold = True With Selection.Interior .Pattern = xlSolid .Color = RGB(31, 78, 121) End With Selection.Font.Color = RGB(255, 255, 255) Columns("F:F").Select Selection.NumberFormat = "[>=10000000]##\,##\,##\,##0;[>=100000]##\,##\,##0;##,##0" Cells.Select Cells.EntireColumn.AutoFit Range("A2").Select

steps.say: Read it from the top. It selects A1 to F1, makes it bold, fills it dark blue and turns the text white. Then it selects column F and sets the lakh number format. Finally it autofits every column and clicks A2.
Press F5 to run it, then Option F11 to look at the sheet. The header is formatted and Net Pay shows lakh commas.

The recorder hard-codes A1 to F1. If next month's report has a seventh column, its header stays plain. Let's write a cleaner version that finds the report's size by itself. Back in the editor, press Command Down to jump to the end.
I'll type the clean version. Current Region means the block of data around A1, however big it is. There's a deliberate mistake in the fourth line: a missing word.

acts.h: Type Sub FormatReportClean() ' Same job without Select: works on any size of report Dim hdr As Range hdr = Range("A1").CurrentRegion.Rows(1) hdr.Font.Bold = True hdr.Interior.Color = RGB(31, 78, 121) hdr.Font.Color = RGB(255, 255, 255) Range("A1").CurrentRegion.Columns(6).NumberFormat = "[>=10000000]##\,##\,##\,##0;[>=100000]##\,##\,##0;##,##0" ActiveSheet.UsedRange.Columns.AutoFit

steps.say: Press F5. Excel stops with run-time error ninety-one: object variable not set. When you store a range in a variable, the line must begin with the word Set. Click End.
Fix it with Replace. Press Command H. Find what: hdr equals Range. Replace with: Set hdr equals Range. Search the current module and click Replace All.

acts.h: Set Replace With to Set hdr = Range

steps.say: Replace is also the safe way to change a value everywhere. Find RGB thirty-one, seventy-eight, one twenty-one, the dark blue. Replace it with RGB zero, one twelve, one ninety-two, a brighter blue. Replace All, then close the box.
Switch back to Excel. On the Developer tab, click Macros, choose FormatReportClean and click Run. The header turns the new blue, and the macro would handle any number of columns and rows.
Pro tip: before editing a macro, copy the whole Sub and paste it below with a new name, so the original still works. And add a comment line saying what the macro does, for the next person.

acts.t:
Pro tip: change macros safely

• Duplicate the Sub, rename it, edit the copy
• Add a ' comment at the top: what, who, when
• Debug > Compile VBAProject catches typos before you run
• Save as .xlsm before testing

steps.say: On a Mac, open the editor with Option F11 or Tools, Macro, Visual Basic Editor. Replace is on the Edit menu, Control H. The Mac editor has no Immediate window docking options, but reading and editing code works the same.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• VBE: ⌥ + F11 or Tools > Macro > Visual Basic Editor
• Insert > Module · Run: F5 (fn + F5) · Edit > Replace (⌃ + H)
• Back to Excel: ⌥ + F11 or click the Excel window
• Some Windows-only objects fail on Mac (lesson S16-04)

steps.say: To recap: macros live between Sub and End Sub, written as object dot property equals value. Use Set when storing a range. Change macros with Replace, and keep a copy of the original.

acts.t:
Recap

• Read: object.property = value
• Range variables need Set
• CurrentRegion instead of fixed addresses
• Edit with Replace; keep the original

steps.say: Your challenge: add one line to FormatReportClean that centres the header text, run it again and check the result. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Add one line to FormatReportClean so the header text is centred.

Answer: sheet S16-02 Done, cell H3

lessons.title: VBA essentials
lessons.mac:
• Same VBA: Dim, If, For, MsgBox, Function
• Save as .xlsm (or .xlam add-in for all workbooks: Tools > Excel Add-ins)
• Edit mode in a cell: ⌃ + U (F2 on Windows)
• UDFs don't work in Excel for the web

steps.say: Collections wants to know which invoices are more than thirty days past due, and finance wants every invoice tagged with its financial year. One short macro marks the overdue invoices in red, and our own worksheet function, FYEAR, fills in the year.
You will learn variables, If Then Else, and a For Next loop, and you will write your own worksheet function. Practice sheet S16-03, recorded in Excel desktop. The code is identical on a Mac.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Variables with Dim
2. If … Then … Else and a For … Next loop
3. MsgBox
4. Your own function: =FYEAR(date)

Practice: sheet S16-03

steps.say: Four building blocks cover most everyday macros. Dim creates a variable. If chooses between two actions. For Next repeats for each row. A Function returns a value you can use in a cell, like any built-in function.

acts.t:
Syntax card

Dim r As Long              ' a whole-number variable
If test Then … Else … End If
For r = 2 To lastRow … Next r
Function FYEAR(d As Date) As String … End Function
Cells(r, "F").Value = "Overdue"

steps.say: Our sheet has twelve invoices with due dates in column D, and an as-on date of thirty-first October in J2. Open the editor with Option F11 and insert a module.

Start with the variables. r is the row number, lastRow is the last filled row, overdueCount is a counter, and asOn is the date in J2. The End xlUp line finds the last row, like pressing Command Up from the bottom of column A.

acts.h: Type Sub MarkOverdue() Dim r As Long, lastRow As Long, overdueCount As Long Dim asOn As Date asOn = Range("J2").Value lastRow = Cells(Rows.Count, "A").End(xlUp).Row

steps.say: Now the loop. For every row from two to the last row: if the as-on date minus the due date is more than thirty days, write Overdue, colour it pink and add one to the counter. Otherwise write OK.

acts.h: Type For r = 2 To lastRow If asOn - Cells(r, "D").Value > 30 Then Cells(r, "F").Value = "Overdue" Cells(r, "F").Interior.Color = RGB(255, 199, 206) overdueCount = overdueCount + 1 Else Cells(r, "F").Value = "OK" End If Next r

steps.say: Last, a message box that reports the count. The ampersand joins the number to the text.

acts.h: Type MsgBox overdueCount & " invoices are more than 30 days overdue.", vbInformation, "Collections"

steps.say: Press F5 to run. The message says seven invoices are more than thirty days overdue. Click OK, and switch to the sheet to see column F filled and coloured.
Now our own function. A common mistake is to type the formula before the function exists. In G2, type equals FYEAR of C2. Excel shows the NAME error, because it doesn't know FYEAR yet.
Back in the editor, press Command Down to go to the end, and type the function. If the month is April or later, the year runs from this year to next. Otherwise it runs from last year to this one.

acts.h: Type Function FYEAR(d As Date) As String ' Indian financial year (April to March) for a date If Month(d) >= 4 Then FYEAR = "FY " & Year(d) & "-" & Right(Year(d) + 1, 2) Else FYEAR = "FY " & (Year(d) - 1) & "-" & Right(Year(d), 2) End If

steps.say: Return to Excel. G2 still shows the old error, so select it, press Control U to edit and press Return to recalculate. It now reads F Y twenty twenty-five, twenty-six. Fill it down to G13 with Command D.

acts.h: Select G2:G13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Pro tip: change the as-on date in J2 and run MarkOverdue again; the statuses update. The FYEAR function updates by itself whenever an invoice date changes, just like SUM.

acts.t:
Pro tip

• Macros run when you run them; functions recalculate by themselves
• Keep inputs like the as-on date in a cell, not inside the code
• Functions can't change other cells or formats, only return a value

steps.say: On a Mac, all of this code runs unchanged, and your FYEAR function works in any cell of this workbook. Save it as xlsm. To use it in every workbook, store it in an add-in, which on a Mac you load from Tools, Excel Add-ins.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Same VBA: Dim, If, For, MsgBox, Function
• Save as .xlsm (or .xlam add-in for all workbooks: Tools > Excel Add-ins)
• Edit mode in a cell: ⌃ + U (F2 on Windows)
• UDFs don't work in Excel for the web

steps.say: To recap: Dim declares variables, If chooses, For Next repeats over rows. A Function gives you a new worksheet formula. If a cell shows NAME, check the function is in a module of this workbook.

acts.t:
Recap

• Dim · If/Then/Else · For/Next · MsgBox
• Function = your own formula (=FYEAR)
• #NAME? → function missing or misspelt

steps.say: Your challenge: change MarkOverdue so the message also shows the total rupee value of the overdue invoices. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Add a variable that totals column E for overdue rows and include it in the MsgBox.

Answer: sheet S16-03 Done, cell L3

lessons.title: What works and breaks in VBA on a Mac
learn: Writing macros that run on both

lessons.title: Office Scripts
learn: Record actions on the Automate tab
Run a script on every new file
lessons.mac:
• Automate tab: Microsoft 365 work/school account, file on OneDrive or SharePoint
• Run and edit scripts on Mac; record in Excel for the web if your build lacks Record Actions
• Scripts are saved in OneDrive > Documents > Office Scripts

steps.say: This is a daily export formatted by an Office Script. Office Scripts are the browser's answer to macros: you record in Excel for the web, the script is saved to your OneDrive, and it runs on Windows, Mac and the web alike.

You will learn to record actions on the Automate tab, read the script it writes, run it on another sheet, and connect it to a schedule. Practice sheets S16-05 and S16-05 Day2. You need a work or school Microsoft 365 account.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. Automate > Record Actions
2. The Code Editor (TypeScript)
3. Run on new data
4. Run automatically with Power Automate

Practice: sheets S16-05 and S16-05 Day2

steps.say: Compared with VBA: Office Scripts use TypeScript, live in OneDrive rather than in the file, work in the browser, and can be triggered by Power Automate. They can't show message boxes or touch your computer's files.

acts.t:
Office Scripts vs VBA

Office Scripts: TypeScript · stored in OneDrive · web, Windows, Mac · Power Automate · business/education accounts
VBA: stored in the .xlsm · desktop only · can use files, message boxes, other apps

steps.say: Go to sheet S16-05. On the Automate tab, click Record Actions. A pane opens and every step from now on is recorded.
Select A1 to F1, press Command B, set the fill to dark blue and the font to white.
Select column F, press Command 1, choose Custom and type the rupee lakh format, then OK.
Select columns A to F and choose Format, AutoFit Column Width on the Home tab. Then View, Freeze Panes, Freeze Top Row.
Click Stop in the pane. Excel shows the script in the Code Editor. Each line is one step, for example get range F colon F, set number format. You can read it without knowing TypeScript.

Here is the common mistake. The recording says get range A1 to F1. If tomorrow's report has a seventh column, its header stays plain. For reports that change shape, edit that line to use the used range of the sheet.
Run it on new data. Go to sheet S16-05 Day2 and click Run in the Code Editor pane. The script works on whichever sheet is active.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S16-05 Day2

steps.say: To run it on every new file, use Power Automate. A flow can start when a file lands in a OneDrive folder, then call Run script with this script. Every export your system drops there is formatted before you open it.

acts.t:
Run on every new file

Power Automate flow:
1. Trigger: When a file is created in a folder (OneDrive for Business)
2. Action: Run script (Excel Online Business) → pick your script

Or: Automate > Automate a Task for ready-made templates

steps.say: On a Mac, the Automate tab appears in Excel for Mac for work and school accounts with the file on OneDrive, where you can run and edit scripts. If recording isn't available on your build, record in Excel for the web; the script then shows up on your Mac too.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Automate tab: Microsoft 365 work/school account, file on OneDrive or SharePoint
• Run and edit scripts on Mac; record in Excel for the web if your build lacks Record Actions
• Scripts are saved in OneDrive > Documents > Office Scripts

steps.say: To recap: Automate, Record Actions, then Stop. Read the steps in the Code Editor. Run on any sheet, or let Power Automate run it on every new file.

acts.t:
Recap

• Automate > Record Actions → Stop
• Code Editor shows one line per step
• Run on any sheet; Power Automate for every new file

steps.say: Your challenge: add a button on the sheet that runs this script with one click. The menu path is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Put a Run button for your script on the sheet.
Hint: the … menu in the Code Editor.

Answer: sheet S16-05 Done, cell H3

lessons.title: Python in Excel: first steps
lessons.mac:
• Formulas > Insert Python, or type =PY(
• Enable Python: Ctrl + Option + Shift + P
• Toggle output: Ctrl + Option + Shift + M · Commit: Ctrl + Return
• Microsoft 365, Current Channel (v16.96+ business); internet required
• Not on iPad or iPhone

steps.say: Python in Excel lets you write a line of Python in a cell and get the answer back on the sheet. By the end of this lesson, three Python cells will load our sales table and give a full statistics summary in one go.

acts.t:
Finished result

• J2: [PY] DataFrame holding the Sales table
• J4: summary statistics for Units and Revenue, as Excel values (count 40)
• J14: total revenue from Python, ₹55,35,400
• Values-only copy on sheet S16-06 Done

steps.say: You will learn to start a Python cell, read a table with the xl function, understand Python objects and Excel values, and avoid the cell-order mistake. Practice sheet S16-06, table Sales.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. =PY cells and xl()
2. DataFrames: Python object vs Excel value
3. describe() for summary statistics
4. Python cells run left to right, top to bottom

Practice: sheet S16-06, table Sales

steps.say: Python runs in Microsoft's cloud, not on your Mac, with libraries like pandas ready to use. xl reads a range or table. A table read with headers equals True becomes a DataFrame, which is Python's version of a table.

acts.t:
Syntax card

=PY(  … Python code …  )
df = xl("Sales[#All]", headers=True)
   xl() reads a range/table · headers=True uses row 1 as column names

Output: Python object (a card) or Excel value (spills onto the grid)
Commit: Ctrl + Enter

steps.say: Click J2 and type equals PY, open bracket. The cell switches to Python mode and shows a green PY tag. On a Mac you can also use Formulas, Insert Python.
Type: df equals xl, open bracket, quote, Sales, square bracket hash All, quote, comma, headers equals True. Then press Control Enter to run it.
J2 now shows PY DataFrame. That card is a Python object: the data is stored in the cell but not spread on the grid. Click the card icon to preview it.

Here is the common mistake. In I2, the cell to the left, type equals PY, df dot shape, and run it. You get a PYTHON error saying df is not defined. Python cells run left to right and top to bottom, so I2 runs before J2 has created df.
Fix it by deleting I2 and always using cells below or to the right of the one that defines df.

Click J4, start a Python cell and type: df, the Units and Revenue columns in double square brackets, dot describe, brackets. Before running, press Control Option Shift M to switch the output to Excel values. Then press Control Enter.

The summary spills onto the grid: forty sales, an average of about 7 point 6 units, and average revenue of about one lakh thirty-eight thousand rupees per sale, with a maximum of seven lakh twenty-eight thousand.

One more. In J14, start a Python cell and type df, square bracket Revenue, dot sum, brackets. A single number comes back straight onto the sheet: total revenue of fifty-five lakh thirty-five thousand four hundred rupees.

On a Mac, Python in Excel needs Microsoft 365 on the Current Channel, version sixteen point nine six or later for business plans; home plans may need the Insider channel. Insert Python is on the Formulas tab. It doesn't work offline, because the code runs in the cloud.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Formulas > Insert Python, or type =PY(
• Enable Python: Ctrl + Option + Shift + P
• Toggle output: Ctrl + Option + Shift + M · Commit: Ctrl + Return
• Microsoft 365, Current Channel (v16.96+ business); internet required
• Not on iPad or iPhone

steps.say: To recap: equals PY starts a Python cell, and xl reads your table into a DataFrame. Switch to Excel values to see results on the grid. Python cells run in reading order, so define things first.

acts.t:
Recap

• =PY( … ) and xl("Table[#All]", headers=True)
• Python object card vs Excel value spill
• describe() = instant summary statistics
• Cells run left→right, top→bottom

steps.say: Your challenge: in J16, use groupby to total Units by Product as an Excel value. Which product sold the most units? The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

J16: =PY( df.groupby("Product")["Units"].sum() ) as Excel value.
Which product sold the most units in April-June?

Answer: sheet S16-06 Done, cell J14

lessons.title: Python in Excel: analysis and charts
lessons.mac:
• Same pandas and matplotlib; runs in Microsoft's cloud
• Output toggle: Ctrl + Option + Shift + M
• Formulas > Python > Reset/Recalculate if results look stale
• Python editor pane: Formulas > Python > Editor (where available)

steps.say: With three short Python cells we'll total July to September revenue by region, build a region by product pivot, and draw a bar chart, all from the SalesQ2 table, and all refreshing when the data changes.

acts.t:
Finished result

• J2: df from table SalesQ2
• J4: revenue by region (Excel values)
• J11: region × product pivot (Excel values)
• J20: bar chart image of revenue by region
• Values-only copy on sheet S16-07 Done

steps.say: You will learn groupby, pivot table and plot in pandas, how to fix a result that stays stuck as a Python object, and when Python is the better tool than formulas. Practice sheet S16-07.

acts.t:
In this lesson

1. groupby: totals by a category
2. pivot_table: two-way summary
3. plot: a chart inside a cell
4. When Python beats formulas

Practice: sheet S16-07, table SalesQ2

steps.say: These three pandas commands do most reporting work. groupby is like SUMIFS for every category at once. pivot table is a PivotTable in one line. plot draws a chart with matplotlib.

acts.t:
Syntax card

df.groupby("Region", as_index=False)["Revenue"].sum()
df.pivot_table(index="Region", columns="Product", values="Revenue", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
df.groupby("Region")["Revenue"].sum().plot(kind="bar")

steps.say: In J2, start a Python cell and load the table: df equals xl, SalesQ2, hash All, headers equals True. Press Control Enter.
In J4, type the groupby: revenue by region, with as index equals False so Region stays a normal column. Press Control Enter.

Common mistake: J4 shows only a DataFrame card, because the output is still a Python object, so you can't chart or reference the numbers. Select J4, press Control U to edit, press Control Option Shift M to switch to Excel value, and Control Enter.
Now the totals spill onto the sheet. South leads with about thirty-two lakh rupees for the quarter.
In J11, build a pivot table: region down the side, product across the top, revenue summed, blanks as zero. Switch it to Excel value before you run it.
For a chart, in J20 type the groupby again and add dot plot with kind equals bar. Run it, and the cell holds an image of the bar chart.
The image fits inside one cell. Click the card icon and choose Display Plot over Cells to see it full size, or Command Shift click the cell to open it in a larger view.

When is Python worth it? When the analysis has many steps, needs statistics or forecasting models, or needs a chart Excel doesn't have. For simple totals, SUMIFS or a PivotTable is quicker for colleagues to check.

acts.t:
When Python beats formulas

✓ Many cleaning and reshaping steps in one place
✓ Statistics, regression, clustering (statsmodels, scikit-learn)
✓ Charts Excel lacks (heatmaps, pair plots with seaborn)
✗ Simple totals and lookups: SUMIFS, XLOOKUP, PivotTables are easier to audit

steps.say: On a Mac, everything here works the same in Excel for Microsoft 365 with Python enabled. The code runs in the cloud, so charts appear as images, and Python cells recalculate when you edit them or press the Recalculate button on the Formulas tab.

acts.t:
Mac corner

• Same pandas and matplotlib; runs in Microsoft's cloud
• Output toggle: Ctrl + Option + Shift + M
• Formulas > Python > Reset/Recalculate if results look stale
• Python editor pane: Formulas > Python > Editor (where available)

steps.say: To recap: groupby gives totals by category, pivot table gives a two-way summary, and plot draws a chart. Switch results to Excel values when you want to use the numbers on the sheet.

acts.t:
Recap

• groupby → totals by category
• pivot_table → two-way summary
• .plot() → chart image in a cell
• Excel value for numbers you'll reuse

steps.say: Your challenge: find the sales rep with the highest revenue in the quarter, using groupby, sum and sort values. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge

Who is the top rep for July-September?
Hint: df.groupby("Rep")["Revenue"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)

Answer: sheet S16-07 Done, cell J22
